name: Dibenzylideneacetone

lead: Dibenzylideneacetone is a yellow organic compound whose conjugated structure absorbs light, which is why it is discussed alongside UV-absorbing molecules.
Its established role is as a ligand for palladium in chemical synthesis; laboratory studies of derivatives cover cancer cells, parasites and fungi.

paras: Two phenyl rings linked through a conjugated ketone chain absorb light and bind metals such as palladium.
It is a research chemical with no approved skin or sunscreen use and no human studies on skin protection.

chain: Proposed as a UV-absorbing chemical class
No finished sunscreen product built on it
angle.text: People interested in sunscreen chemistry note that dba is a conjugated, light-absorbing molecule, the same general feature that lets filters shield skin. It is a research chemical, and its use in skin protection is a concept rather than a product.

lead: Dibenzylideneacetone (dba) is a bright-yellow crystalline organic compound with the formula C17H14O, made by condensing acetone with two molecules of benzaldehyde. Its two phenyl rings joined through a conjugated chain give it strong light-absorbing character, which is why it is sometimes mentioned alongside UV-absorbing, sunscreen-type molecules.[1]

In practice it is best known as a laboratory reagent: a ligand for palladium, forming complexes such as tris(dibenzylideneacetone)dipalladium(0), widely used in cross-coupling chemistry.[1] It is not a listed ingredient in consumer sunscreens or skincare products in the sources reviewed, and its appearance-related interest centres on its light-absorbing structure.
Published research on dba and its derivatives covers cancer cell lines, parasites and fungi, and imaging agents, all at laboratory stage.[2][3][4][5]

paras: The trans,trans isomer is the stable, common form, melting at roughly 110 to 111 C. It is insoluble in water and dissolves in ethanol, acetone and chloroform.[1]
It is prepared by a base-catalysed Claisen-Schmidt condensation, first described in 1881 by Rainer Ludwig Claisen and Charles-Claude-Alexandre Claparede.[1]

No studies found. Laboratory research includes derivatives tested against cervical cancer cells, Trypanosoma brucei parasites and a fungus that infects tomatoes, and a palladium complex studied in cancer models; dba scaffolds have also been explored for radiolabelled Alzheimer's imaging agents.[2][3][4][5][6]

Dba-based compounds are used as starting points in medicinal chemistry. One report described dba sensitising tumour cells to the TRAIL cytokine through reactive oxygen species.[7] These studies do not address use on skin or as a sunscreen.

timeline.event: Claisen and Claparede report the acetone-benzaldehyde condensation that yields dba.[1]
